title: Install a plug-on breaker in a load center: load end hooked on the rail, jaw pressed fully onto the bus stab
instruction: Install the new breaker in space 4 of the unpowered, unwired load center.
context: Electricians (O*NET 47-2111, about 0.8 million workers) install breakers whenever a circuit is added or a breaker is replaced. A plug-on breaker goes in the maker's way: its load (wire terminal) end hooked under the mounting rail at the panel's outer edge, then its line end pushed in until its plug-on jaw is fully on the bus stab. A breaker left part way on its stab makes a poor contact that heats and arcs; one not hooked on the rail works loose. The panel's spaces are numbered on its label: odd on the left, even on the right, from the top.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table (x forward, y left); the layout is the same in every trial. Fixed: a 19 mm plywood wall board (60 cm wide, 50 cm tall) standing upright on the table across the robot's view, its face at x 42, centred on y -6. Screwed to it as on a wall: a Square D Homeline HOM48L125GC 4-space load center, not wired to any supply (painted steel enclosure 37.6 cm tall, 22.6 cm wide, 9.7 cm deep, about 3 kg), its back against the board, its bottom 1 cm above the table, centred on y -6, its top (main lugs) up and its dead front off; its plastic interior's breaker-mounting face is at x 39. Its left-hand column (spaces 1, 3) is at +y and its right-hand column (spaces 2, 4) at -y, the bus stabs down the middle and the mounting rails along both outer edges. Spaces 1 and 3 hold Square D HOM120 breakers; spaces 2 and 4 are empty. Space 4 (the right-hand column, the lower row) is centred at y -10.5, 18.5 cm above the table. Loose: a new Square D Homeline HOM120 breaker (1-pole, 20 A; 2.54 W x 7.95 H x 7.57 D cm; black plastic housing, copper jaw; about 120 g), OFF, lying on its back (mounting face down) on the table at x 22, y -26, its line (jaw) end pointing left (+y).
scoring: Measured on the breaker against its seated place in space 4; checked at the end. 1.0: in space 4, its jaw fully on the stab and its mounting face against the interior at both ends (a 1 mm feeler does not pass behind either end), its load end hooked under the rail's lip, square (within 2 degrees), no part of either gripper within 1 cm of it, the breaker still, for 1 s. 0.5: hooked on the rail of space 4 with its jaw on the stab's full blade but not home (an end standing more than 1 mm out), or seated with a hand still on it or not yet still. 0.25: hooked on the rail of space 4, its jaw not on the stab's blade (resting on it). 0: anything else, for example the jaw pushed onto the stab with the load end not under the rail's lip, or the breaker in another space.
reset_notes: Remove the breaker the maker's way: pull its line end out until the jaw lets go of the stab, then lift its load end off the rail; lay it back on its back on the table at the marked spot, line end to the left, handle OFF. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: All contact, no rules: the jaw is two copper shoes on springs (12 N preload each, 4000 N/m, 2.0 mm apart) that must spread over the 3.2 mm stab, whose top tapers at 15 degrees; friction 0.3. The load end's hook slot and the rail's lip (reaching 4.5 mm in) are collision geometry with 1 mm clearances. In the simulator a 40 N push on the line end leaves the jaw part way on; 60 N seats it. The spring and the inner shapes are our estimates. Boxes.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (the right hand picks the breaker up and moves it about over the table, then reaches into the enclosure; the breaker is never hooked on the rail); demo: 1.0 (success at step 529)
